newsitem.title: ITALY: Albanian parties sign election pact.
newsitem.headline: Albanian parties sign election pact.

text.p: Albania's main political parties pledged on Monday to ensure a free and fair general election in six days' time but one key leader said he still feared fraud at the polls.
The "Pact for the Future of Albania", signed in Rome in the presence of international media, pledged that the parties would work for stable and democratic government.
It recognised the need for a coalition government after Sunday's vote and said the opposition would be entitled to hold key watchdog positions in parliament.

Fatos Nano, leader of the main opposition Socialist Party and one of the signatories, said "as a gentleman and a very serious politician" he would respect the results even if his party did not win but quickly added in response to a question:
"I also confirm there is no possibility that my party will lose the election."

The four-point agreement was signed at the Sant'Egidio Community, a Roman Catholic peace group, by Nano as well as by Tritan Shehu, the chairman of President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party and Skender Gjinushi of the Social Democrats.

"The most important thing is that with this kind of (agreement) we could have further influence in calming down the population and creating the necessary climate to rebuild the country...," Nano told reporters after he signed.
Shehu said he hoped the agreement would help foster "co-operation among all parties needed to resolve the grave problems of Albania".

But Nano told reporters that he feared that despite intensive monitoring planned by the international community there was still a possibility that "the only alternative left to some still-active gangs and structures of secret police acting under Berisha's orders could be (to) destroy ballots".
He said he believed the polls had to close before dark otherwise this would become "a very serious weapon for the night-moving structure of still-existing secret police".
More than 1,500 people have been killed in Albania, Europe's poorest country, since the start of the year in unrest that began with a revolt over the collapse of shady savings schemes.
About 50 people have died in the past week alone as the campaign for Sunday's general election draws to a close.

Signatories to the accord promised to conduct the remainder of the campaign "according to the standards of correct political dialogue, avoiding any violence that obstructs freedom of movement and of the expression of political ideas".
"The solution to the grave crisis which Albania is going through... depends on the free and fair conduct of the elections on June 29, 1997," the accord said.

"It is only on this condition that the electoral results, confirmed by the international community, will be incontestable and respected not only by our political parties but, above all, by the Albanian people throughout the country," it said.

The leaders of two smaller parties, Sabri Godo of the Republican Party and Hysen Selfo of the rightist National Front, attended the Rome ceremony. Sant'Egidio officials said they did not sign the document out of respect for many other tiny parties which were not represented.
The Democratic Party is defending a huge parliamentary majority won in a general election last year which both Albania's opposition and Western observers denounced as unfair.
Berisha was forced in March to agree to Sunday's early election and to the appointment of a multi-party government led by the Socialists after a rebellion in the south of the country.
Rioters looted weapons from depots and for several days Albania was on the brink of anarchy.
A 7,000-strong multinational peacekeeping force has also been deployed in the Balkan state but gangs still roam many roads and some areas elude control of authorities.
